Update: Thank you for the follow-up. I want to clarify that my concern was not about needing to schedule an appointment. The issue was being told that providing the Cytopoint injection without a wellness visit was “illegal,” when my understanding is that it is best practice, not a legal requirement. This was part of an already prescribed treatment plan for my pet, who had recently been seen at your clinic and had documentation in her file. I did schedule an appointment but ultimately canceled because the interaction left me unsettled. My feedback is really about how the situation was communicated and the strong emphasis on a wellness visit despite the already prescribed vet documented plan. What was most disappointing was how quickly we were dismissed as patients - our files were removed within minutes of the conversation. After five years with the clinic, that felt disheartening and not reflective of the relationship we thought we had built.

I don’t typically leave reviews, but I wanted to share my experience after recently deciding to move my pets to a new veterinary practice.

I have been a long-time client (5yrs) and have always tried to do the right thing for my dogs. Even during the last couple of years when work and finances were challenging, I still prioritized bringing my pups in and making sure they received their yearly care and treatments. Their health has always come first for me.

Unfortunately, over the last two years the experience at the clinic has started to feel different. There seemed to be increasing pressure to add services and a strong push around wellness visits, particularly for one of my dogs who already comes in more frequently because of allergies.

The moment that ultimately led me to leave happened during my most recent interaction. I was told it was illegal for my dog to receive her Cytopoint injection without a wellness visit. After asking a few more questions, I was able to get an appointment scheduled, but by that point the interaction had already left me feeling uncomfortable. This was the second or third similar interaction. I ended up canceling and finding another veterinarian.

What surprised me most was when I called back to cancel and mentioned I would be moving to a new vet, the response was simply, “Okay, thank you.” After being a long-time client who consistently invested hundreds of dollars per visit across multiple pets—even during difficult financial periods—it felt surprisingly dismissive.

I want to be clear that the veterinary staff themselves have always been kind to my pets, and I truly appreciate the care they’ve provided over the years. However, the overall experience has increasingly felt more transactional than relationship-based, which is hard when you view your pets as family and would do anything for them.

I understand the veterinary industry is facing economic pressures, but many pet owners are as well. Sometimes what clients need most is transparency and a little grace. Saying something is “illegal” when it is actually a best practice can feel frustrating and erodes trust.

I’m sharing this feedback in hopes it’s helpful, because every pet owner deserves to feel supported and respected when they’re trying to do the best for their animals.

I took my dog there for surgery to remove a fatty lump which I’ve now learned is more cosmetic than medically necessary. Not only did he remove another lump the size of a pencil eraser, he ensured me “it’s not cancer but just to be safe”; turns out he said (after he submitted to lab to examine slide, see below) oh yes it IS cancer. My girl had to go for a recheck on her stitches; he and I discussed a few other things related to cancer and I had asked for a nail trim of one nail; me with a cancer dx for my girl and precious little money tho I’d been making it happen with CPHC for my three dogs for YEARS (visits, allergy shots and expensive senior bloodwork annually at 7 because I was told it was necessary at that age; my dogs are 16/14/12 now tyvm), and my dog about her nails, we were a little anxious. He seemed to be rushing, told me -quote- “I don’t have time for this” as he yanked her paw to him, and she bled. To stop the bleeding he sent in a tech.

If you’re too busy, why do the nail trim yourself even if your clients didn’t visibly need an extra minute to calm down after discussing cancer you originally assured us wasn’t present? Also, who gave the okay to make a second cut into my dog without my permission, much less pass cost into me creating an undue hardship for our already struggling family, without again, asking or at least telling. There was no acute medical emergency ongoing; I *should* have had the option for deciding some things, many times even apart from that incident, it seems.

After years of seeing Drs. Denum & Izard, but Kyzar being head doc there, I quit on the spot. I was disgusted to learn a bit later 1. the place where each incision was made? Never healed up too great, visually speaking, and now things hang lower to possibly snag more than that little fatty lump ever did, and 2. Dr. K apparently goes to church. Even the worst of them preach compassion, especially to “the least” of the world. That can go a long way even when you don’t ask permission or act ill when rushed. I’ll pray Kyzar learns that, otherwise step down and just be a business owner, not interface with customers. Not to mention be honest about what’s necessary versus what’s good to have but optional m, like senior blood panels at 7 “just to see where they’re at “.
